Specify a Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE) Pipeline

Source: R/tmle_spec.R
tmle_spec.Rd

Creates a progressive-disclosure specification for cross-fitted Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (CV-TMLE). At Level 1, only outcome, treatment, covariates, and estimand are needed; sensible defaults for 10-fold cross-fitting, Super Learning, adaptive positivity truncation, and bounded logistic fluctuation are enabled automatically. At Level 2, attach custom recipes, parsnip specs, workflows, workflowsets, and rsample objects using the set_*() verbs.

Usage

tmle_spec(
  outcome,
  treatment,
  covariates = NULL,
  censoring = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  estimand = "ate"
)

Arguments

outcome

Tidyselect specification of the outcome column. May be numeric (continuous or 0/1 binary) or a 2-level factor/logical.

treatment

Tidyselect specification of the treatment/exposure column. For standard causal estimands ("ate", "att", "atc", "rr", "or", "ey1", "ey0"), must be binary (0/1, logical, or 2-level factor). For Modified Treatment Policies (shift(), scale_tx()), numeric continuous.

covariates

Optional tidyselect specification of baseline confounders \(W\). Defaults to NULL, which automatically selects all columns in data other than outcome, treatment, censoring, id, and weights.

censoring

Optional tidyselect specification of the observation/non-censoring indicator \(\Delta \in \{0, 1\}\) (where 1 = observed, 0 = censored). If omitted and outcome contains NAs, tidytmle automatically introduces \(\Delta = \mathbb{I}(\neg\text{is.na}(Y))\) and models informative missingness via \(C(A, W) = P(\Delta = 1 \mid A, W)\).

id

Optional tidyselect specification of a clustering/grouping identifier. Automatically triggers grouped cross-validation and cluster-robust influence-function standard errors.

weights

Optional tidyselect specification of a case-weights column (supporting hardhat::importance_weights(), hardhat::frequency_weights(), or positive numeric vectors).

estimand

Causal estimand(s) to target: one or more of "ate", "att", "atc", "rr", "or", "ey1", "ey0", or a Modified Treatment Policy created by shift() or scale_tx(). Defaults to "ate".

Value

An object of class "tmle_spec".

Details

How TMLE Works ("Predict, Then Target")

Standard machine learning regression models \(\bar{Q}^0(A, W) = E[Y \mid A, W]\) optimize global prediction accuracy rather than the bias-variance trade-off for a causal contrast such as the Average Treatment Effect (ATE). Conversely, inverse-probability weighting (IPW) relies entirely on the propensity score \(g(W) = P(A = 1 \mid W)\) and blows up in variance when positivity is stressed.

As synthesized in Schuler & Rose (2017) and Luque-Fernandez et al. (2018), TMLE resolves both weaknesses in two stages:

  1. Predict: Estimate the initial outcome surface \(\bar{Q}^0(A, W)\) and treatment propensity \(g(W)\) (plus missingness/censoring \(C(A, W)\) when outcomes are missing) using cross-validated Super Learning.

  2. Target (Fluctuate): Construct arm-specific Clever Covariates \(H_1(A, W) = \mathbb{I}(A = 1) / g(W)\) and \(H_0(A, W) = \mathbb{I}(A = 0) / (1 - g(W))\) (including censoring weights when outcomes are missing) derived from the Efficient Influence Function (EIF). By default (fluctuation = "logistic"), outcomes are mapped to (0, 1) and fluctuated via arm-specific weighted-intercept canonical logistic models \(\text{logit}\,\bar{Q}^*(a, W) = \text{logit}\,\bar{Q}^0(a, W) + \epsilon_a\) using weights \(H_a\) (matching target.gwt = TRUE). Classical unweighted Clever-Covariate fluctuation (\(\text{logit}\,\bar{Q}^0 + \epsilon_1 H_1 + \epsilon_0 H_0\), matching target.gwt = FALSE) is available via fluctuation = "logistic_covariate". Both nudge initial predictions until the sample mean of each component EIF solves the zero score equation.

This makes TMLE a doubly robust, locally efficient substitution estimator: point estimation remains consistent if either \(\bar{Q}\) or \(g\) (and \(C\) under missingness) is consistently estimated, while EIF-based Wald confidence intervals and semiparametric efficiency hold when both nuisance models converge fast enough that their second-order product remainder is \(o_p(n^{-1/2})\).

References

van der Laan, M. J., & Rubin, D. (2006). Targeted maximum likelihood learning. The International Journal of Biostatistics, 2(1), Article 11.

Schuler, M. S., & Rose, S. (2017). Targeted maximum likelihood estimation for causal inference in observational studies. American Journal of Epidemiology, 185(1), 65–73.

Luque-Fernandez, M. A., Schomaker, M., Rachet, B., & Schnitzer, M. E. (2018). Targeted maximum likelihood estimation for a binary treatment: A tutorial. Statistics in Medicine, 37(16), 2530–2546.

Examples

df <- sim_causal_cohort(n = 150, outcome_type = "binary", seed = 42)
spec <- tmle_spec(
  outcome = y,
  treatment = a,
  covariates = c(age, sex, starts_with("lab_")),
  estimand = c("ate", "rr", "or")
)
spec
#> 
#> ── Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE) Specification ──
#> 
#> • Outcome to measure: y
#> • Treatment / exposure: a
#> • Confounders adjusted for: c(age, sex, starts_with("lab_"))
#> • Causal question(s): "ate", "rr", and "or"
#> • Cross-fitting: TRUE (10-fold out-of-sample)
#> • Safety guardrails: bounds = "adaptive" | calibration = "logistic"
#> Next: pass to fit(data = your_data) to estimate causal effects.
